explainBack.question: Why would an AI trained on ordinary preserved pathology slides give worse answers on frozen sections, and how does CRISP avoid that?
explainBack.answer: Frozen sections are rushed: tissue is frozen and sliced mid-surgery, so ice and speed change how cells look compared with slides preserved slowly in chemicals and wax. A model trained only on the wax-preserved appearance has never seen frozen morphology, so its learned patterns mismatch and accuracy drops. CRISP avoids this because it was pretrained on a large collection of actual frozen-section images, so the appearances it learned are the appearances it is asked to judge.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The article's statement that most existing AI learned from usual preserved slides whose look differs from frozen tissue (P003), grounded in P002's description of the two preparations; the paper's page-12 statement that FFPE-trained models 'may lack exposure to frozen section morphology.'
explainBack.assessment: The article supports this answer accurately: P002 establishes the appearance difference and P003 gives the training-distribution mechanism, matching the source without overstating.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A hospital buys a skin-lesion AI that matched dermatologists in studies using clinic dermoscopy images, then proposes letting triage nurses run it on ordinary smartphone photos and claims it will improve melanoma outcomes.
unseenTransfer.question: Using this article's mechanism, what two distinct problems should the hospital's evaluation committee raise?
unseenTransfer.answer: First, domain shift: like FFPE-trained models on frozen tissue, an AI trained on dermoscopy images has never seen smartphone lighting, focus and colour, so its matched-specialist accuracy may not carry over — it needs validation on the actual input type. Second, performance is not outcomes: even genuine accuracy parity in a reader-style comparison does not show patients fare better; only a study that changes care and follows patients — the interventional trial the CRISP authors say they still need — can establish that.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P003's training-appearance mismatch mechanism and P005's distinction between observed performance, simulated deployment and an interventional outcomes study.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's two core ideas transfer cleanly and completely to this new case, confirming the mechanism was taught rather than merely asserted.

frozen-specific.reason: P003 matches PDF page 12: most existing foundation models are built on FFPE specimens which 'differ fundamentally from frozen sections in both preparation and tissue morphology,' and CRISP was pretrained specifically on frozen-section images (50 million patches from frozen slides).

result.reason: Page 13 and the discussion report CRISP 'consistently achieved superior performance' over competing foundation models across prospective external cohorts, and the reader study found the senior pathologist's operating point on CRISP's ROC curve, 'indicating comparable overall performance under the evaluated conditions' — matching P003's 'beat other AI models' and 'matched the senior specialist overall,' with the article's 'overall' preserving the qualification.

simulation-limit.reason: The core claim is supported: the paper reports a simulated deployment analysis on an independent set of 100 SYCC cases measuring end-to-end time (196.4s vs 292.6s), the study was observational not interventional, and the authors state 'a fully prospective interventional study is still necessary.' One wording nit: the article says '100 selected cases' while the Methods describe '100 consecutive cases,' an independent set — 'selected' could wrongly imply cherry-picking the paper explicitly avoided.

factualIntegrity.reason: Every material claim in P002, P003 and P005 traces to specific paper passages (pages 12, 13, 20, 23, 33–34) with attribution and limits retained; the sole 'selected' vs 'consecutive' slip is minor and does not change the claim's substance.

freshnessReviewability.reason: The story cites a Nature Medicine paper published 2026-09-10 (landing page metadata), accessed 2026-09-12, with checkable claims; the study's observational nature and pending interventional work are disclosed (P005).

datedChange.reason: This is a single newly published study; the article correctly frames it as new evidence with no conflation of older events, and distinguishes retrospective training data from the new prospective evaluation (P003).

consequenceAndUncertainty.reason: Consequences are concrete (decision support during surgery, P004) and uncertainty survives fully: P005 and P006 state explicitly that performance parity does not prove better treatment or outcomes.

learningDisposition.rationale: One qualified claim: replace '100 selected cases' with '100 consecutive cases' (or 'an independent set of 100 cases') to match the Methods and avoid implying cherry-picking. All other claims fully supported.
